summary: Initial discovery focused on jurisdictional evidence, legal‑hold/logging constraints, and whether Verdant should target Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, or Private. Customer concerned about cross‑border logs, eDiscovery holds, key custody, and audit evidence for regulators. Redwood AE/SE explained hosting options, fallback behavior, key management alternatives, and logging redaction patterns; agreed to follow up with security docs and pilot pricing.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-02-23 11:30 AM PT / 46m; Attendees: Samira (Redwood), Ethan (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood), Maya (Verdant CTO), Luca (Verdant Legal), Aria (Platform), Ben (Security)

[00:00:00] Samira (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick agenda — residency, logs, legal‑hold, and then we can talk hosting options and pilots. Maya, want to kick off with your top constraints?

[00:00:15] Maya (Verdant): Yeah thanks. Uh, main thing is we operate in both the UK and US, and our clients include retail investors and a handful of institutional accounts. Regulators ask for clear evidence of processing location and we have to produce logs for investigations — sometimes on pretty short notice. We're trying to understand if we can use Redwood Hosted or if we need Dedicated/Private to satisfy eDiscovery and data jurisdiction requirements.

[00:00:45] Ethan (SE): Totally. Two quick clarifying q's — are you required to keep transaction‑level logs inside a specific jurisdiction, or is it more that the audit trail and copies of logs need to be producible within that region?

[00:00:58] Aria (Platform): It's both. For some clients we must ensure raw logs never leave the UK. For others we just need the ability to produce evidence within 48 hours. Also legal hold — when a case opens, we might need to preserve model interactions for months or years regardless of standard retention.

[00:01:20] Samira (AE): Understood. Quick high‑level: Redwood Hosted gives the fastest time‑to‑value but is multi‑tenant and logs are centralized per region. Redwood Dedicated is a tenant‑isolated pool (reserved capacity) that can be region pinned. Redwood Private gives you a customer‑controlled control plane — VPC or on‑prem — so you can keep logs and keys under your tenancy.

[00:01:45] Luca (Legal): When you say "logs" — what are we talking? Request/response payloads, token streams, call metadata, full trace? For eDiscovery we usually need an immutable chain: timestamps, request id, and sometimes the text.

[00:02:05] Diego (SE): Good q. By default Redwood collects request metadata, model variant, latency, and anonymized telemetry. Full request/response retention is configurable per account; we can turn on full logging for a tenancy but we also offer redaction hooks and prefix/KV cache options so PII doesn't get persisted. In Dedicated/Private we can also restrict storage region and integrate with your S3 in that region or forward logs to your SIEM.

[00:02:35] Ben (Security): Can you walk through key custody? If we need to ensure no plaintext model inputs are stored outside our control, we need customer KMS or HSM integration.

[00:02:45] Ethan (SE): Yes — Redwood supports customer‑managed keys via KMS, and for Private we can integrate with on‑prem HSMs. For Hosted we do offer envelope encryption with our KMS; customers that require cryptographic separation typically prefer Dedicated with KMS key ownership or Private where keys never leave their environment. There was a small delay; sorry — I need to correct the phrase: for Hosted we currently provide CDC… I mean, centralized key handling — it's not ideal for regulatory work.

[00:03:10] Maya (Verdant): And is that documented? Like, auditors will ask for the chain of custody. We need a diagram.

[00:03:18] Samira (AE): Absolutely — we'll send SOC 2 and ISO attestation, and a control map showing where logs live for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. We'll include a network diagram for Private/VPC.

[00:03:30] Luca (Legal): Two more legal‑y points: 1) legal hold: if litigation or regulatory inquiry arises, can we freeze or export stored interactions on short notice? 2) eDiscovery chain of custody — do you provide signed timestamps or hashes we can rely on?

[00:03:45] Diego (SE): For Dedicated/Private, yes we can implement retention lockers and export paths. We can also surface an immutable object store in the customer's region and emit hashes (SHA256) of items on write to support chain‑of‑custody claims. For Hosted, some of that requires workarounds — we can supply exports and signed manifests but it's less turnkey.

[00:04:10] Aria (Platform): What's the typical delay for exports? If we need to produce 30 days of conversations within 72 hours, is that realistic?

[00:04:20] Ethan (SE): For Dedicated/Private — yes, 72 hours is realistic; for Hosted it depends on the retention policy and whether we need to run a cross‑region export. We'll call that medium risk.

[00:04:35] Ben (Security): Audit logging and integration with our Splunk instance — do you push logs or do we pull? We prefer push over private peering via a forwarder.

[00:04:45] Diego (SE): We support both. Common pattern is streaming logs to customer S3 in region via VPC endpoint and then your SIEM pulls; alternatively we can ship events to a HTTPS endpoint with auth or push to Kafka/Splunk using a forwarder. In Private deployments we can colocate the forwarder inside the VPC for lowest leak surface.

[00:05:10] Maya (Verdant): A practical question — if we choose Dedicated in eu‑west and some traffic is US based, can you route US traffic to US region while ensuring EU data never leaks? We have hybrid workloads.

[00:05:25] Samira (AE): Yes — routing policies can pin a model or tenant to a region and you can set routing rules by customer ID, IP, or token. Redwood can also do fallback to compatible models in another region only if explicitly allowed; otherwise the request fails with soft error. We call that region locking.

[00:05:50] Luca (Legal): About retention windows — our compliance policy says 7 years for certain records. Is it feasible to set retention per‑data‑type? Like immediate logs 30 days (hot), legal‑hold copies cold for up to 7 years?

[00:06:05] Diego (SE): Yes — tiered retention is standard. We can set hot vs cold buckets and apply lifecycle policies. For legal hold, we can move items into an immutable bucket with object locking for mandated windows.

[00:06:25] Aria (Platform): You mentioned redaction hooks — how reliable are they? If a user pastes PII into a prompt, can we automatically scrub it before it hits persistent storage?

[00:06:35] Ethan (SE): We have a few options: 1) client side — preprocess and redact before sending; 2) runtime hooks — call your PII scrubber via function call before persisting; 3) post‑ingest redaction job. Runtime hooks are preferred for low latency, but client side gives you most control. Redaction is heuristic so we'd recommend a hybrid approach and policy validation in the pipeline.

[00:07:00] Ben (Security): Any chance for escrowed keys for long term audit? Our security team wants an escrow option where keys for archived buckets are held with a 3rd party.

[00:07:12] Diego (SE): We can support key escrow for archived material in Private deployments via a partner HSM. For Hosted it's more challenging but possible with contractual addendum and a dedicated key provisioning flow. We'll need legal to scope.

[00:07:28] Luca (Legal): Great. Also, are there any known gaps from a regulator perspective? For example, if a regulator in the UK asks for the raw prompts, would Redwood be able to guarantee they were never replicated outside country?

[00:07:40] Samira (AE): With Private or region‑pinned Dedicated, yes — you can guarantee residency. Hosted, again, depends on whether you accept multi‑region backups for DR. We can offer region‑locked backups as part of an enterprise package.

[00:07:55] Maya (Verdant): Latency is also a factor. Some of our UI flows need sub‑400ms response times. If we go Private, what's the expected tradeoff vs Hosted?

[00:08:05] Ethan (SE): Private colocated near your infra will usually beat Hosted due to network proximity, but you lose Redwood's multi‑region edge optimizations. For Dedicated, we can reserve GPUs in region and tune batching to meet 200‑400ms for small seq lengths; cost will be higher per token. We'll share benchmarks.

[00:08:30] Aria (Platform): Are there existing customers in finance you've worked with on legal hold? Anything you can share as a pattern?

[00:08:38] Samira (AE): Yes — we had a mid‑size wealth manager who did a Dedicated pilot, they pin regions and used S3 with object locking for legal hold. They also pulled hashes into their compliance ledger for chain of custody. We'll anonymize that case study and include it in the docs pack.

[00:08:55] Luca (Legal): Ok, on SLAs and evidence — will we get logs that show request ID, user ID, timestamps, and model variant as part of exports? We need those fields for regulatory submission.

[00:09:07] Diego (SE): Yes — those fields are standard metadata. We also can include token counts, latency, and model artifacts version. If you need additional metadata we can add custom headers.

[00:09:25] Ben (Security): About legal hold — say we freeze items; can we also block deletion at the API level to prevent accidental purge?

[00:09:33] Ethan (SE): Yes — immutability flags prevent delete operations while legal hold is active. That is supported for Dedicated and Private object stores.

[00:09:45] Maya (Verdant): Are there any audit logs for operator access inside Redwood? Our auditors want a view of who accessed logs and when.

[00:09:55] Diego (SE): For Dedicated and Private we provide operator audit trails. For Hosted we provide a control plane audit log, but operator visibility is limited for multi‑tenant infra. We can also integrate with your SIEM for alerting on operator actions.

[00:10:15] Samira (AE): Quick commercial note — Dedicated typically has a 3‑6 month ramp and an annual contract; Private has longer lead times and higher engineering uplift. For a compliance‑first pilot, many customers start with a short Dedicated pilot region‑pinned and then evaluate Private if legal asks for full control.

[00:10:36] Aria (Platform): For the pilot, what would you need from us to size it?

[00:10:42] Ethan (SE): Sample QPS, typical sequence length, and peak concurrency. Also we need worst‑case retention requirements — if you're keeping many months of full interactions that's storage heavy.

[00:10:55] Maya (Verdant): We can share a traffic snapshot and retention policy. Luca will pull legal hold scenarios.

[00:11:06] Luca (Legal): One last tricky item — cross‑border eDiscovery: if we preserve UK items in an immutable bucket in the UK, but a US regulator requests data, do you support an export path with audit trail? We need export logs showing chain of request and approval.

[00:11:22] Diego (SE): Yes — we can build an export workflow with approval gates and signed manifests. We'll include export audit logs and hashes as part of the proof. There is some implementation work to wire approval flows to your internal ticketing system — we can scope that in the security deep dive.

[00:11:42] Ben (Security): Can we get SAML + SCIM to sync roles and ensure RBAC across the Redwood Console?

[00:11:48] Ethan (SE): We support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning; RBAC is customizable per tenancy in Dedicated/Private. Hosted has a default role set but supports mapping to SAML groups.

[00:12:05] Samira (AE): Let's wrap with clear next steps. We'll send the requested docs (SOC2/ISO/network diagram), Ethan/Diego will prep a dedicated pilot estimate and security deep‑dive deck. Luca will send legal‑hold examples. Anything to add?

[00:12:20] Maya (Verdant): No, that covers it. We'll schedule the security deep dive next week if possible.

[00:12:28] Samira (AE): Great — thanks, everyone. We'll follow up with the doc packet and Doodle for a slot.

[00:12:35] (crosstalk)

[00:12:40] End of recording.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis‑hears (SAML -> "smell" in the auto transcript), proper nouns sometimes wrong (Verdant transcribed as Verdence in one snippet), timestamps approximate. The transcript contains normal disfluencies, interruptions, and clarifying questions.
